content.title: About
content.content: Raw carrots are a root vegetable belonging to the Apiaceae family. Grown worldwide, they are known for their sweet taste, crunchy texture, and bright orange color, which comes from a high beta‑carotene content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Carrots were first domesticated in Central Asia over 5,000 years ago.
Originally, carrots were purple, yellow or white; the orange variety became dominant in the 17th century in the Netherlands.
Beta‑carotene in carrots is converted in the body to vitamin A, essential for vision.
Carrots can grow in almost any soil type but prefer light, well‑drained ground.
Raw carrot sticks are a popular healthy snack for children.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene is a precursor of vitamin A, supporting vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Raw carrots are low‑calorie, making them suitable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: In addition to beta‑carotene, carrots provide vitamin C, lutein and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium in carrots helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of raw carrot can cause gas or discomfort in individuals with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic carrots, it is advisable to wash them thoroughly to remove any chemical residues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw carrots can be eaten as sticks, grated into salads, added to smoothies, used as a dip accompaniment, or served as a side dish. For a softer texture, briefly blanch the carrots.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store carrots in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, placed in a perforated bag. When kept properly, they stay fresh for 2–3 weeks. Remove any leafy tops to extend shelf life.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese is a dairy product made by coagulating milk, separating the curds from the whey, and pressing the curds. Over 1,500 varieties exist, differing in flavor, texture, aging process, and the type of milk used (cow, goat, sheep).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese has been produced since ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt.
The world’s most expensive cheese, “Pule,” can cost over $1,000 per kilogram.
Swiss cheese caves maintain constant temperature and humidity, ideal for aging.
Many regions celebrate a “cheese day” where enthusiasts sample multiple varieties.
Cheese ranges from soft (brie, camembert) to hard (cheddar, parmesan).

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese provides a high amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Complete protein in cheese supports tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheese contains vitamins B2, B12, and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic cultures
items.content: Some aged cheeses contain live cultures that benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Beneficial fatty acids
items.content: Conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) in cheese may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after eating cheese.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Many cheeses are salty, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Cheese is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to mold growth and harmful bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cheese can be sliced for snacks, added to salads, pastas, casseroles, used in sauces, or enjoyed melted in fondue or as a topping. Pair it with fruit, nuts, or wine for a balanced snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cheese in the refrigerator, wrapped in parchment paper and then in foil or a sealed container. Hard cheeses keep for months, soft cheeses for about a week. Check for unwanted mold before consumption.

chicken-or-turkey-a-la-king-with-vegetab.title: Chicken or Turkey a la King with Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken or turkey a la King is a classic American dish featuring tender pieces of poultry in a rich vegetable sauce. This version excludes carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy vegetables, as well as potatoes, cream, white sauce, and any soup‑based stock.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the early 20th century and quickly became a staple in U.S. diners.
The name “a la King” comes from the King’s Café, where the recipe was first popularized.
Traditional sauce is made with butter, flour, and cream; this version uses oil and a light broth instead.
Shallots, garlic, thyme, and sage are common aromatics that enhance the flavor.
It can be prepared in a single pot, saving time and dishes.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Cooking without cream and using vegetable oil keeps the dish relatively low‑calorie.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is rich in niacin and vitamin B6, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables such as bell pepper, zucchini, and cauliflower add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If using store‑bought broth, watch the salt level to avoid excess sodium intake.

items.title: Digestive load
items.content: Large portions of protein can be heavy on the stomach for those with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, typically over rice, quinoa, or whole‑grain pasta. Garnish with fresh herbs like parsley or dill for added brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat with a splash of broth to restore a creamy texture.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese and vegetables (excluding dark green and tomatoes), fat added

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese and vegetables is a dish made from beaten eggs cooked on a skillet with added fat (butter, oil, or other). The vegetables can include bell pepper, onion, mushrooms, zucchini and other non‑dark‑green or tomato varieties. Cheese (cheddar, mozzarella, feta, etc.) gives a creamy flavor and boosts the protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are a complete protein source, containing all essential amino acids.
Cheese adds calcium and phosphorus, important for bone health.
The vegetables used provide B‑vitamins, vitamin C and antioxidants.
Added fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
Cooking omelets in a pan dates back to ancient Roman culinary practices.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Protein from eggs and cheese helps build and repair muscle tissue, especially with regular exercise.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin D
items.content: Egg yolks contain vitamin D, which is important for immune function and bone health.

items.title: Bone strengthening
items.content: Calcium from cheese and phosphorus from eggs work together to maintain bone mineralization.

items.title: Eye health
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in yolk protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: The added fat provides a sustained source of energy and promotes satiety.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, cheese, or dairy fat.

items.title: High cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol levels should moderate portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively high in calories due to fat and cheese, so portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese often contains salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt or reduced‑fat varieties.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Beat eggs with a splash of milk or cream, stir in grated cheese and chopped vegetables. Heat a skillet, melt the fat, pour in the egg mixture and cook, stirring, until the desired consistency is reached. Season with pepper, paprika, or dried herbs as desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Eggs and cheese should be kept in their original packaging at 1‑4 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate‑covered Graham crackers are crisp whole‑grain biscuits coated with a layer of milk or dark chocolate. They combine the sweet richness of chocolate with the mild, slightly nutty flavor of the classic Graham cracker, making them a popular snack and dessert garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Graham crackers were created in the United States in the late 19th century as a healthier alternative to sweet biscuits.
Originally they were used as the base for cheese “tea sandwiches” in traditional American tea culture.
Chocolate coating appeared in the 1970s when manufacturers began experimenting with new flavors.
The crackers are often used in recipes for cheese balls and layered desserts because of their sturdy texture.
In the U.S. more than 200 million packages of chocolate‑covered Graham crackers are sold each year.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: The crackers contain whole‑grain flour, providing dietary fiber and slow‑release carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Malted grains in the cracker contribute iron, which is essential for blood formation.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Chocolate, especially dark, is rich in flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The mix of carbs and a modest amount of fat supplies quick and sustained energy.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin production, which can enhance mood.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The crackers contain wheat, so they may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The chocolate coating adds sugar, which can be problematic for diabetics or those monitoring weight.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Combining biscuit and chocolate makes the product calorie‑dense; moderation is recommended.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Milk chocolate may cause reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chocolate‑covered Graham crackers can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to yogurt, ice cream, or used as layers in cakes and desserts. They also make convenient bite‑size toppings for various dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight package. For longer shelf life keep refrigerated to prevent chocolate bloom. Discard if you notice a rancid smell or texture changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Lettuce (Lactuca sativa) is a leafy vegetable widely used in fresh dishes. In this version the leaves are slightly wilted and are drizzled with a bacon‑based dressing that adds a smoky, savory flavor and a crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Slight wilting can concentrate the leaf’s aroma, giving a richer taste.
Bacon dressing is often finished with a touch of maple syrup to balance salty and sweet notes.
Lettuce belongs to the Asteraceae family and is one of the oldest cultivated crops.
The combination of fresh greens and smoked meat is popular in American cuisine, especially in Caesar‑style salads.
Lettuce leaves can be up to 95% water, making them an excellent source of hydration.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Lettuce provides a high amount of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: One cup of lettuce contains about 15 calories, making it ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate supports normal cell division and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lettuce contains lutein and zeaxanthin, which protect the eyes from UV damage.

items.title: Bacon adds protein
items.content: The bacon dressing contributes additional protein and iron.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Bacon is often salty, so the dish can be high in sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Bacon contains saturated fats and should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: People with pork allergy or sensitivity to animal products may react to the dressing.

items.title: Bacterial spoilage
items.content: Wilted lettuce can spoil faster; keep it refrigerated and consume within 1‑2 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad cold, drizzling the bacon dressing just before serving. Add toasted nuts, pumpkin seeds, or a splash of lemon juice for extra balance.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the lettuce leaves in an airtight container in the fridge, separate from the dressing. Keep the bacon dressing in a sealed jar and use within 3‑4 days.
